source: Tuite, Kevin. A Short Descriptive Grammar of the Svan Language. manuscript version dated 12 February 2004.
claim: The sketch explicitly distinguishes Upper Bal, Lower Bal, Lent’ex and Lashx dialect areas and bases descriptions partly on the author's fieldwork in Georgia (1985–86, 1988, 1991, 1995).
geography: Upper Enguri and Cxenis-c’q’ali valleys, Georgia

claim: Tuite characterizes the Svan consonant inventory as essentially Classical Georgian plus /j/ and /q/; Svan lacks distinct /v/ but has /w/.
Zhghent’i reported a distinct voiced uvular /G/ in roughly two dozen, often expressive or onomatopoeic lexemes, but Kaldani and Tuite did not elicit that consonant from their speakers.

Phonologically contrastive vowel length occurs in Upper Bal and Lashx, though minimal pairs are few; Lower Bal and Lent’ex lack synchronic length but preserve morphophonological evidence for earlier long vowels.
Tuite regards vowel length as reconstructible for Proto-Svan, while treating a Proto-Kartvelian quantity opposition as uncertain and disputed.
Relative to Georgian, Svan adds a back unrounded mid-high vowel transcribed /´/, low-front /æ/, and front rounded /œ y/.
/œ/ and /y/ are often realized diphthongally as /we/ and /wi/; some analysts therefore decline to treat them as independent phonemes.

Upper Bal has nine short vowel qualities plus long counterparts (18 vowel phonemes); Lower Bal and Lent’ex have the same nine qualities without length; Lashx has six qualities, each short and long (12 vowel phonemes).

Word-initial clusters are tightly restricted, essentially to harmonic clusters, consonant+/w/ clusters, and a small historically derived class; this contrasts with much freer Georgian initial clustering.
Inherited or borrowed initial clusters outside the permitted classes are broken up with epenthetic vowels or repaired by vowel prothesis; Tuite illustrates epenthesis with a Russian loan.

The cluster restriction interacts with verbal person prefixes: xw-/x- delete before root-initial consonants, /w/ can metathesize, and other person-marker plus consonant sequences can be repaired by epenthetic schwa.
Unlike its severe initial restrictions, Svan permits very heavy word-final consonant clusters.
Zhghent’i attributes Svan's heavy final clusters to historical weakening and loss of vowels in word-final syllables; Tuite reports this attribution rather than presenting it as uncontested fact.
Tuite argues that Svan morphophonemics point to an earlier strong mobile accent, citing loss of final segments, syncopation of short vowels in even-numbered syllables, and some vowel lengthening.

Many Svan long vowels are analyzed as innovations from vowel contraction, compensatory lengthening, or phonological environments such as a following sonorant; occasional nominal-to-verbal lengthening may be accent-related.

Aorist S1/2sg vs S3/pl alternations in ablauting and strong verbs reflect an inferred historical accent shift from root to prefix, producing stem-vowel deletion, preverb lengthening, or shortening of long root vowels depending on the class.
Traditional poetry is reported to lack long and umlauted vowels, show relatively little reduction, and use filler vowels—including default /i/—to satisfy an often eight-syllable line requirement.
lect_scope: traditional poetic register across dialect areas

claim: In all dialects except Lent’ex, every nonfinal even-numbered vowel is liable to syncope/reduction: /o u/ reduce to /w/, /i e/ delete but can umlaut the preceding vowel, and /a æ ´/ delete without residue.
When reduction would create the sequence /CVSC/ (S = sonorant), schwa is inserted, coupling vowel reduction to cluster repair.

Long vowels resist reduction. In Lower Bal, which synchronically lacks length, vowels corresponding to Upper Bal/Lashx long vowels are likewise reduction-resistant, evidence for an earlier distinction (possibly length or accentuation).

Lent’ex lacks the every-second-vowel reduction rule; /i/ and occasionally /u/ can instead reduce in restricted penultimate contexts, which Tuite interprets as evidence for a different early accentuation pattern.
At a vowel-final word or outer preverb followed by a vowel-initial word (except initial /i u/), a vowel may delete and the second vowel can undergo compensatory lengthening.
Palatal umlaut fronts /a o u ´/ under influence of /i/ or /e/ in the following syllable; traces occur in all four dialects, with Lashx less affected.
A second type of umlaut lowers high /i e/ to /æ/ or /a/ under influence of a following /a/ or /w/.

Tuite summarizes gradient historical/dialectal umlaut hierarchies: targets /a/ > /o/ > /u/, short > long, root > affix; triggers /i/ > /e/ > /æ/, reduced > unreduced, short > long, and underlying trigger vowels > derived ones.

Tuite reports Kaldani's three-stage chronology: an early intensive umlaut affecting all dialects before the earliest 13th–15th-century Svan attestations; a later narrower rule absent from Lashx; and continuation of that later rule in some Lower Bal and Lent’ex subdialects after it ceased elsewhere.

Labialization from the first-person marker can metathesize onto the root-initial consonant or round a vowel; in a Lower Bal variety it can migrate farther to the second root consonant, and direction varies by dialect.
Suffixal /r/ is prone to dissimilation to /l/ when the root already contains /r/; the pattern is especially common in Lower Svan, while Upper Svan more readily tolerates successive /r/ syllables.
Tuite relays Zhghent’i's examples of voicing dissimilation in borrowed/proper-name material, including a form derived from Georgian K’wirik’e and 'Christ' from krist’e.

True ablaut, excluding alternations attributable to umlaut or reduction, is restricted to one verb class representing roughly 15% of verbs in the cited Svan-English dictionary and retains parts of Proto-Kartvelian ablaut with later changes.

Tuite lays out two analyses of ablaut-vowel history—one deriving /´/ as reduced underlying /i/, another treating /´/ as underlying and /i/ as historically umlauted—and explicitly favors the second on optative and umlaut-behavior evidence.
